item.title: SBI data breach explained: What are your rights if personal data is leaked?
item.description: SBI's reported data leak has raised questions about customer privacy. Here's what Indian laws require banks to do, whether affected customers can seek compensation and how they can protect themselves ...
item.dc:creator: Mini Raghav
item.content:encoded: The State Bank of India (SBI) has admitted that it found 3,897 records containing personally identifiable information of customers on the dark web. The information reportedly included names, mobile numbers, dates of birth, email and residential addresses, customer identifiers and metadata linked to loan records. This raises some larger questions: whether the bank complied with its existing security obligations, what reporting requirements apply and what customers can do if the exposure causes them harm. What does the IT Act say about a data breach? The Information Technology (IT) Act, 2000, is an important part of India's existing legal framework for data protection and cybersecurity. Section 43A provides for compensation when a company handling sensitive personal information fails to maintain reasonable security practices, and this failure causes wrongful loss or gain. However, the fact that customer information has appeared online does not automatically prove that the bank was negligent. The legal requirements must be met before compensation can be awarded. The Information Technology (Reasonable Security Practices and Procedures and Sensitive Personal Data or Information) Rules, 2011, also set out requirements for handling sensitive information and maintaining adequate security measures. Two other provisions may apply, depending on how the data was obtained or disclosed. Section 66 covers certain computer-related offences, including unauthorised access, when the acts specified under Section 43 are committed dishonestly or fraudulently. Section 72A deals with the unlawful disclosure of personal information obtained under a lawful contract, where the intention or knowledge required by law is established. In simple terms, investigators must first determine how the information was accessed, whether anyone disclosed it unlawfully and whether the conditions for a legal violation have been met. DPDP Act explained: What does India's new data protection law say? The Digital Personal Data Protection (DPDP) Act, 2023, creates a framework for regulating how organisations collect, use and protect digital personal data. However, the Act is being implemented in stages. Under the commencement notification issued on November 13, 2025, its core provisions on data processing, security safeguards and breach notifications are scheduled to take effect on May 13, 2027. The DPDP Rules, 2025, also have a phased implementation schedule. These core work should therefore not be treated as fully enforceable against SBI for an incident identified in October 2026. Once Section 8(5) takes effect, organisations that determine how and why personal data is processed must take reasonable security measures to prevent breaches. Section 8(6) requires them to notify the Data Protection Board of India and affected individuals of a breach, as prescribed by the rules. Section 33 provides for monetary penalties for specified violations. A failure to take reasonable security safeguards can attract a penalty of up to ₹250 crore, which is not static but is a variable amount. The distinction is important to look at because these future obligations cannot simply be applied to the SBI incident before they come into force. RBI's cybersecurity rules: What must a bank do? Banks are responsible not only for keeping customers' money safe but also for protecting the personal and financial information they collect. The Reserve Bank of India's (RBI) 2016 Cyber Security Framework in Banks and its 2023 Master Direction on Information Technology Governance, Risk, Controls and Assurance Practices set standards for security, risk management, internal controls and incident response. Under these requirements, banks must put systems in place to detect potential threats, investigate security incidents and take steps to prevent similar incidents in the future. In other words, banks cannot wait for a cyberattack to happen before thinking about data security. Protecting customer information is an ongoing responsibility. In the SBI data breach case, the question is whether the bank followed the required security measures and responded appropriately after learning about the suspected exposure. The exposure alone does not prove that the bank violated RBI rules; that conclusion requires evidence. CERT-In's six-hour reporting rule: When must a breach be reported? The Indian Computer Emergency Response Team (CERT-In), India's national cybersecurity agency, operates under Section 70B of the IT Act. Under directions issued on April 28, 2022, organisations covered by the rules must report specified cybersecurity incidents, including data breaches and leaks, within six hours of noticing them or being informed about them. These organisations must also maintain system logs, which can help investigators understand what happened during a cyber incident. SBI said it received alerts about the suspected exposure on October 16 and publicly disclosed it on October 21. These dates raise questions about the reporting timeline, but do not prove a violation. To assess compliance, it is necessary to establish when the incident was detected, when it became reportable and when the authorities were notified. Can customers claim compensation if their data is leaked? Customers may seek remedies under the IT Act and the Consumer Protection Act, 2019, depending on the circumstances. Under Section 43A of the IT Act, compensation may be available if a company failed to maintain reasonable security measures for sensitive personal information and that failure caused wrongful loss or gain. The Consumer Protection Act, 2019, may provide another option. If a bank's failure to protect customer information amounts to a deficiency in service, an affected customer may be able to file a consumer complaint, provided the legal requirements are met. For example, a customer who loses money through fraud after personal information is exposed may have evidence of financial loss. Another customer whose information was leaked but who has suffered no identifiable harm may face a different legal situation. Data breach versus financial fraud: What should customers do? Exposed personal information does not necessarily mean that money has been stolen. However, fraudsters can use leaked details to make phone calls and messages appear genuine. Customers should be cautious about unexpected calls, links and requests to update banking details. They should never share passwords, PINs or one-time passwords with callers claiming to represent their bank. Anyone who suspects an unauthorised transaction should contact the bank immediately. Suspected cyber fraud can also be reported through the national helpline, 1930, or by going to the National Cyber Crime Reporting Portal.

item.title: RBI's ₹2.5 trillion liquidity infusion sends mixed signals: SBI Research
item.description: SBI Research says the RBI's ₹2.5 trillion liquidity injection amid calibrated monetary tightening sends contradictory signals and could complicate monetary policy transmission ...
item.dc:creator: Subrata Panda
item.content:encoded: The Reserve Bank of India’s (RBI’s) decision to inject ₹2.5 trillion into the banking system through repo auctions, even as it signals a calibrated monetary tightening cycle, has sent contradictory signals on liquidity management, according to a report by SBI Research. The report said the RBI appeared to be balancing multiple, potentially conflicting objectives, with its liquidity operations raising questions about the consistency of its policy stance. “We are getting contradictory signals from RBI on the liquidity management front,” the report said, pointing to the central bank’s continued emphasis on calibrated tightening alongside three repo auctions conducted from October 19 onwards to inject a total of ₹2.5 trillion into the banking system. The report questioned whether the RBI was moving away from calibrated tightening towards what it described as “mildly calibrated tightening”. It argued that the simultaneous use of liquidity injection and withdrawal measures could complicate the transmission of the central bank’s monetary policy signals to financial markets. SBI Research said the RBI had maintained the requirement for daily call money rates to remain at 99 per cent of the policy rate, alongside regular open market operation (OMO) and variable rate reverse repo (VRRR) operations. These measures, it said, indicated that the central bank was pursuing a calibrated tightening approach. The substantial liquidity injection through repo auctions, however, appeared inconsistent with that approach, particularly after the RBI’s October monetary policy placed greater emphasis on inflation risks and the need for policy recalibration. The report highlighted that while concerns about financial stability might have influenced the liquidity operations, the RBI would be better served by avoiding a two-way liquidity management policy involving simultaneous injection and withdrawal. SBI Research argued that such a two-way approach was more appropriate for exchange rate management than for liquidity management. It reiterated its recommendation for widening the liquidity adjustment facility (LAF) corridor, which, it said, could act as an automatic stabiliser during periods of uncertainty. Despite the decline in US Treasury yields, SBI Research highlighted that Indian government bond yields were unlikely to fall significantly, with the 10-year government security yield expected to remain elevated at around 7.6 per cent at the higher end for now. The report said the RBI’s liquidity injection and its decision to cancel all Treasury bill auctions could be interpreted by market participants as attempts to fine-tune movements in yields. However, it argued that domestic bond yields would remain under pressure because of elevated crude oil prices and the likelihood of a renewed rise in US Treasury yields. The report added that the spread between Indian and US government bond yields, at around 250 basis points, was finally moving towards normalisation. Meanwhile, SBI Research said the rupee had appreciated by around 2 per cent from its low of 96.8 per dollar recorded on May 20, while remaining marginally weaker than its level on March 31, 2026. The report said the RBI’s decision to move the operating rate to the upper end of the policy corridor was appropriate in signalling a tightening cycle. It argued that the move had helped reinforce the monetary policy signal while supporting the currency.

item.title: Apple's iPhone Duo hits stores in face of short supply, high demand
item.description: The iPhone lineup is Apple’s largest moneymaker, generating roughly half of the company’s revenue. And the Duo is the biggest single design change in the device’s nearly two-decade history. Though the ...
item.dc:creator: Bloomberg
item.content:encoded: By Mark Gurman Apple Inc. has already shown there’s a strong appetite for its $2,000-and-up foldable iPhone Duo. Now it needs to meet that demand. The new device goes on sale Friday, with the first shipments reaching Apple retail stores around the world. It also will begin arriving at the homes of customers who ordered quickly enough to secure day-one deliveries. The launch is bringing back a once-familiar sight: lines outside Apple stores. Such crowds have largely disappeared in recent years after Apple, retailers like Best Buy Co. and wireless carriers began maintaining enough inventory to fulfill most orders through home delivery or appointment-based store pickups. This time is different. Supplies for preorders were so limited that many customers hoping to get the Duo on launch day have little choice but to line up and see whether their local store has any inventory available. Apple is allocating a small portion of its stock for those people.  At the company’s flagship Fifth Avenue store in New York City, where top Apple executives typically open the doors to buyers, there was a line of customers without preorders that reached more than a few dozen people by the early evening on Thursday. There were similar lines in Asia and Australia. As one of the most expensive mainstream smartphones ever sold, the Duo had raised questions about just how much demand there would be. But early adopters, resellers and everyday Apple fans have demonstrated that the interest is there. The iPhone lineup is Apple’s largest moneymaker, generating roughly half of the company’s revenue. And the Duo is the biggest single design change in the device’s nearly two-decade history. Though the company wasn’t first to market with a foldable phone, it looks to gain an edge with a more polished product built for Apple fans. Rather than a repeat of the lackluster debut of the Vision Pro headset nearly three years ago, the Duo’s launch is shaping up to be a throwback to the iPhone introductions of old — when demand far outstripped supply. That’s the case even with device prices reaching as high as $3,199 for models with 2 terabytes of storage. Though the Duo’s cost sets a record for a mass-market smartphone, Apple’s competitors such as Samsung Electronics Co. have been raising prices as well. Shortages of memory chips and other components have made consumer electronics more expensive across the board.  Consumers placing new orders for the Duo on Apple’s website are now being offered delivery at the end of January, though some early buyers have seen their January shipping estimates move up to as soon as November or December. The delays mark some of the lengthiest for a new Apple product in the company’s modern era. The phones are difficult to produce because of their advanced hinge and new display technology. They’re also only built in a limited number of facilities in China. Apple expanded production in recent years for its traditional iPhones, including to India, which has helped with supply.  Apple reports its quarterly earnings results on Nov. 2, but the period won’t include sales of the Duo because the period concluded around the end of September. It will reflect early sales of iPhone 18 Pro and Pro Max models, which debuted on Sept. 18. Other new versions, such as the entry-level iPhone or the updated Air, won’t go on sale until next year, Bloomberg News has reported. That marks a change in the company’s usual release schedule, a move meant to help spread out revenue across the year.

item.description: Obeda Pro and Obeda Plus are made by a different manufacturer than the original Obeda injectable, supplies of which were halted in July after Dr Reddy's discovered an impurity in active ingredients ...
item.content:encoded:
Home / Industry / News / Dr Reddy's launches new generic Ozempic brands amid Obeda supply disruption

Dr Reddy's launches new generic Ozempic brands amid Obeda supply disruption Obeda Pro and Obeda Plus are made by a different manufacturer than the original Obeda injectable, supplies of which were halted in July after Dr Reddy's discovered an impurity in active ingredients

Dr Reddy's is likely to discontinue supplies of Obeda and instead focus on Obeda Pro and Obeda Plus

Reuters HYDERABAD 3 min read Last Updated : Oct 23 2026 | 3:36 PM IST

Listen to This Article

Dr Reddy's Laboratories has expanded its portfolio of generic versions of Ozempic with two new brands, according to product photographs and marketing materials reviewed by Reuters, after supply disruptions hit sales of its original Obeda injection in India's fast-growing semaglutide market. Obeda Pro and Obeda Plus are made by a different manufacturer than the original Obeda injectable, supplies of which were halted in July after Dr Reddy's discovered an impurity in the active ingredient. Dr Reddy's is likely to discontinue supplies of Obeda and instead focus on Obeda Pro and Obeda Plus, several distributors told Reuters. "The company said there were some technical issues with Obeda injectable, and they recalled stocks from us. They said they would instead supply Obeda Pro," a drug distributor said on condition of anonymity as they were not authorized to speak to the media.   The development and launch planning for products such as Obeda Pro and Obeda Plus were under way well before the July supply disruption issues, Dr Reddy's said in response to a Reuters request for comment. "The presence of multiple semaglutide brands and manufacturing arrangements reflects the breadth of our portfolio strategy and should not be interpreted as evidence that one product was launched to replace another," it said. Dr Reddy's recalled Obeda injection in July "for technical evaluation," according to a notice reviewed by Reuters. The company did not reply to a Reuters question on whether the recall was related to the impurity. An oral version of the drug was not recalled. Dr Reddy's launched Obeda - a generic version of Novo Nordisk's diabetes drug - in India in March after semaglutide lost patent protection in the country, setting off a race among domestic pharma companies to launch lower-cost versions of the drug. Semaglutide, which suppresses appetite, is also the active ingredient in Novo's blockbuster weight-loss drug Wegovy. Obeda Plus and Obeda Pro are available in different dose strengths, just like Ozempic and Wegovy. Research firm Pharmarack estimated in March that the domestic market for semaglutide drugs will grow to 80 billion rupees ($843.99 million) by 2030. Dr Reddy's said in July that supplies of Obeda injections would be unavailable until November. Analysts warned at the time that the company risked losing market share in India's increasingly competitive semaglutide market if supplies were not restored quickly. Dr Reddy's did not reply to a question on whether it had resolved the impurity issue. Packaging materials reviewed by Reuters showed Obeda was manufactured by contract manufacturer OneSource Specialty Pharma. Obeda Pro and Obeda Plus, which began appearing in the market in late July according to supply invoices reviewed by Reuters, are manufactured by Hetero Labs. Hetero Labs and OneSource Specialty Pharma did not respond to requests for comment. Dr Reddy's sold about 442,000 units of generic semaglutide through September in India, according to research firm Pharmarack. By comparison, India's largest drugmaker Sun Pharma sold 151,000 semaglutide units.

(Only the headline and picture of this report may have been reworked by the Business Standard staff; the rest of the content is auto-generated from a syndicated feed.)
